# 2 Maccabees Chapter 11 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 11 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_011_page_001.jpg

---

**11:1** Shortly after this, Lysias — the king's guardian, close relative, and chief minister — was furious over what had happened. He assembled some eighty thousand soldiers, all his cavalry, and marched against the Jews.

**11:2** His plan was to turn Jerusalem into a Greek city, to tax the temple the way other foreign shrines were taxed, and to auction off the high priesthood to the highest bidder every year.

**11:3** He had no regard for God at all. He was drunk on his numbers: tens of thousands of infantry, thousands of cavalry, eighty war elephants.

**11:4** He entered Judea and advanced on Beth-zur, a strong position about five stadia from Jerusalem, and began to besiege it.

**11:5** When Maccabeus and his men heard that Lysias was besieging their fortifications, they broke into weeping and lamentation — they and all the people — crying out to the Lord to send a good angel to rescue Israel.

**11:6** Maccabeus himself was the first to arm. He urged the others to put their lives on the line alongside him and come to the aid of their fellow Jews. They all went forward together, burning with eagerness.

**11:7** While they were still near Jerusalem, a horseman appeared riding at their head, dressed in white, with golden weapons gleaming.

**11:8** Every one of them praised the God of mercy and was filled with such courage that they felt ready to take on not just men, but ferocious beasts and walls of iron.

**11:9** They advanced into battle with their ally from heaven — the Lord had had mercy on them.

**11:10** They threw themselves at the enemy like lions and cut down eleven thousand infantry and sixteen hundred cavalry, routing the rest entirely.

**11:11** Most of the survivors were wounded. Lysias himself escaped with his life — barely — and fled in shame.

**11:12** But Lysias had a clear head. He thought over what had happened and recognized the truth: the Hebrews were unbeatable because a mighty God was fighting for them. So he sent word to them

**11:13** and proposed a settlement on fair terms, promising to persuade the king to deal favorably with them on all outstanding matters.

**11:14** Maccabeus agreed to everything Lysias proposed, since the welfare of the whole people was at stake. And everything Maccabeus submitted in writing to Lysias on behalf of the Jews, the king approved.

**11:15** The letter that Lysias wrote to the Jews read as follows:

**11:16** "Lysias to the Jewish people, greetings. John and Absalom, your envoys, have delivered your written requests and asked for a response on the matters listed.

**11:17** I have laid before the king whatever needed to go before him, and he has approved what was allowable.

**11:18** If you remain loyal to the government, I will work to advance your interests going forward.

**11:19** I have asked these men, and my own representatives, to discuss the specific details with you in person.

**11:20** Farewell. Year 148, the twenty-fourth of Dioscorinthius."

**11:21** The king's letter read as follows:

**11:22** "King Antiochus to his brother Lysias, greetings. Since our father has gone to join the gods, it is our wish that the people of our kingdom be free to go about their own affairs without interference.

**11:23** We have been informed that the Jews refuse to accept our father's program of Greek customs and prefer to live by their own traditions, and they are requesting that those traditions be respected.

**11:24** It is therefore our decision that this people too shall be left in peace. We decree that their temple be returned to them and that they live by the customs of their ancestors.

**11:25** Send word to them, then, and give them your assurances of goodwill, so that they may feel reassured and get on with running their own affairs."

**11:26** The king's letter to the Jews read as follows:

**11:27** "King Antiochus to the council of elders of the Jews and to the rest of the Jewish people, greetings. I trust you are well — as we are.

**11:28** Menelaus has told us that you wish to come home and get back to your own affairs.

**11:29** Accordingly, all who return home by the thirtieth of Xanthicus will receive full pardon.

**11:30** The Jews will be free to use their own food and observe their own laws as before, and none of them will face any consequences for things done out of ignorance.

**11:31** I am also sending Menelaus to speak with you.

**11:32** Farewell. Year 148, the fifteenth of Xanthicus."

**11:33** The Romans also sent the following letter:

**11:34** "Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, Roman legates, to the Jewish people, greetings.

**11:35** We concur with what Lysias the king's kinsman has granted you.

**11:36** As for the matters he referred to the king — deliberate on them and send someone to us promptly so we can put your case in the best possible light. We are heading to Antioch.

**11:37** Send people quickly so we know where you stand.

**11:38** Farewell. Year 148, the fifteenth of Xanthicus."
